title: What is geocaching?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain geocaching: its origins in the 2000 end of GPS selective availability (after Korean Air Lines Flight 007 and Reagan's directive), Dave Ulmer's first cache in 2000 and the "take some stuff, leave some stuff" model, and how the hobby works. They cover required gear (GPS receiver, a post-1984 topographic map, supplies), cache etiquette (log books, trinkets, no drugs or alcohol, maintaining caches, avoiding private, historic, and park land), variants (multi-caches, mystery caches, letterbox hybrids, virtual caches, hitchhiker caches and geocoins), lingo (CITO, TNLN, FTF, muggles, spoilers), and a Philadelphia Franklin Institute King Tut promotion. They close with a plug for the webcast and blog and two listener mails.
topics: Franklin Institute King Tut geocaching promotion

segments.title: Opening banter and housing prices
segments.summary: Chuck mentions his wife's soap business and a grand opening, Josh mentions Detroit house prices, and they introduce geocaching after listener requests.

segments.title: Origins: Flight 007, selective availability, and GPS
segments.summary: Korean Air Lines Flight 007 was shot down after entering Soviet airspace, prompting Reagan to make GPS commercially available. The public signal had intentional degradation (selective availability) of about 300 feet, which Clinton ordered removed, happening in 2000 rather than 2006.

segments.title: Dave Ulmer's first cache
segments.summary: Handheld GPS devices hit the market, and Dave Ulmer hid a container and posted its coordinates online with the phrase 'take some stuff, leave some stuff.' Mike Teague was the first to find it, and the hobby was initially called GPS stash hunt before the name geocaching was coined, credited to Matt Stum.

segments.title: What geocaching is and mapping requirements
segments.summary: Geocaching is described as a treasure hunt using GPS coordinates from websites. Participants need a GPS receiver, internet access, and a topographic map made after 1984 because the WGS 84 datum replaced the North American datum of 1927, to avoid mismatches with GPS.

segments.title: Gear and choosing a cache
segments.summary: Recommended gear includes flashlight, bug spray, sunblock, hiking boots, water, and extra batteries. Geocaching.com is named as a main site, and beginners are advised to choose a nearby cache.

segments.title: Cache contents, etiquette, and hiding rules
segments.summary: Caches contain trinkets such as CDs and handmade items; drugs and alcohol are not allowed. Hiders should label caches with contact info, since a cache in a New Hampshire supermarket caused a panic. The log book is essential, and caches should be kept clean and maintained. Caches should avoid private land, national parks, historic and archaeological sites, and high-traffic areas.

segments.title: Variations and lingo
segments.summary: Variants include multi-caches, mystery caches, letterbox hybrids, and virtual caches. Lingo includes CITO (cache in trash out), TNLN (took nothing left nothing), FTF (first to find), muggles, and spoilers. A Philadelphia Franklin Institute King Tut promotion in 2007 used a geocaching game.

segments.title: Plugs, further reading, and listener mail
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh plug the Wednesday webcast and blog, recommend Strickland's and others' articles, and read two listener mails: one about an older woman at a gym, and one about Wisconsin city pronunciations from a pen pal named Danielle.
